918.title: Peshawar joins the kingdom
918.hook: the frontier city is brought into the kingdom
918.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Peshawar in histories of Maharaja Ranjit Singh's reign and in the stories of Hari Singh Nalwa, the general who held the north-west frontier.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kashmir, and your line was the valley. Did you find a sheltered place to rest? Today we go west, to the other end of the map. Day nine hundred eighteen.

Peshawar is a market town where the plains run out. Caravans unload in its bazaars: horses, dried fruit, carpets from beyond the hills. Behind the city, the road climbs west toward Afghanistan. Traders came down that road. Armies came down it too, again and again, into the Punjab. A city that sits at the mouth of a pass like that is never just a city. It's a door. Whoever holds it decides who comes in. Today: Peshawar joins the kingdom.
screen: `A CITY AT THE MOUTH OF A PASS.` → `TRADERS AND ARMIES.` → `A DOOR, NOT JUST A CITY.`

segments.voice: First, the long approach. Peshawar didn't fall in a day. For years it sat between the Sikh kingdom and the Afghan rulers, paying tribute to Lahore at times, slipping back at others. Sikh histories tell of battles on the plains around it and of the slow pull of the city toward Lahore. Second, the general. You met him a few days ago: Hari Singh Nalwa, who held the frontier. In the way Sikh histories tell it, he was the one who brought Peshawar fully into the kingdom and then governed the region. He built forts, among them the fort at Jamrud near the pass, where he would later fall. Third, what it meant. With Peshawar held, the kingdom's edge sat at the foot of the Khyber. The door that armies had used to come down into the Punjab was now held from Lahore. Sikh tradition remembers this with pride: the road that had brought invaders now had a Sikh guard on it. Fourth, the cost of an edge. A border city is never quiet. Peshawar had its own Pashtun leaders with their own loyalties, and the Afghan rulers wanted it back. Holding it meant troops, forts and constant watch. An edge is where a kingdom stands guard and where it can be struck, both at once. A fort at the mouth of a pass, its gate facing the hills: that's the edge.
screen: `YEARS OF PULL BETWEEN TWO POWERS.` · `HARI SINGH NALWA BRINGS IT IN.` · `A SIKH GUARD ON THE INVADERS' ROAD.` · `AN EDGE IS STRONG AND EXPOSED.` · then, large: `THE EDGE.`

segments.voice: Two minutes at the edges. Sit and let your breath settle. Now think of the edges of your own world: the last street you know well, the people at the far side of your circle, the subjects you avoid, the hour of the day you never see. Pick one edge. Rest your attention there for a few breaths. Don't push past it. Just notice what's on the other side, and how it feels to stand at the line. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Peshawar, the city at the mouth of the Khyber, pulled toward Lahore for years and brought into the kingdom under Hari Singh Nalwa. Today's word.

Your line: the edge. Today, take one small step toward an edge of your world: a new street, a new voice, a question you usually skip. Then come home and notice what you brought back. Day nine hundred eighteen.

919.title: The Koh-i-Noor
919.hook: the great diamond comes to Lahore in 1813 from an exiled Afghan king
919.howItsDone: Sikhs meet the Koh-i-Noor in histories of Maharaja Ranjit Singh's court, and in the Japji's picture of jewels within the mind.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Peshawar, the city at the mouth of the pass, and your line was the edge. What did you find at the edge of your world? Today, something small enough to hold in one hand. Day nine hundred nineteen.

A king without a kingdom arrives in Lahore. He's Shah Shuja, once ruler in Kabul, now driven out, with his family and what's left of his treasure. He needs shelter and help. And he has with him one stone that had passed from ruler to ruler, a diamond so large it had its own name. The Maharaja wants it. The exile doesn't want to let it go, and he has nowhere else to turn. Today: the Koh-i-Noor.
screen: `AN EXILED KING IN LAHORE.` → `ONE STONE WITH ITS OWN NAME.` → `WHO WILL HOLD IT?`

segments.voice: First, the name. Koh-i-Noor is Persian, and it's usually given as the mountain of light. A stone named like a mountain. Second, how it changed hands. The histories don't agree on every detail, and Afghan and Sikh accounts tell it differently. In the way it's usually told, Shah Shuja and his wife had come to the Maharaja for help, and the diamond became the price of that help. Some accounts say it was handed over under pressure, after delay and hard bargaining. So the stone came to Lahore not in a battle but in a bargain with a man who had little left to bargain with. That's worth sitting with. Third, what the Maharaja did with it. Tradition says he wore it on his arm in an armband, and showed it at court on great days. The mountain of light became part of how Lahore looked to visitors: a kingdom that could hold what Kabul and Delhi had held before. And fourth, the question underneath: what counts as a jewel? In Guru Nanak's hymns, jewels can stand for something inside. In the Japji, he says the mind holds jewels, gems and rubies, if you listen to even one teaching of the Guru. A king's diamond is real, and beautiful, and worth a fortune. The Gurus point at a different kind of worth. Both stand in today's story, side by side.
screen: `THE MOUNTAIN OF LIGHT.` · `A BARGAIN WITH AN EXILE.` · `WORN ON THE MAHARAJA'S ARM.` · `THE JEWEL THE GURUS POINT TO.` · then, large: `WHAT IS PRECIOUS.`

segments.voice: Two minutes with what's precious. Sit, and let your breath slow down. Ask yourself, without rushing: what would I call precious? Let the first answers come, and let them go. Then wait for the quieter ones underneath: a person, a memory, a kind of peace, something no one could buy from you. Choose one. Hold it in your mind the way you'd hold a stone in your palm, carefully, turning it to the light. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
The Koh-i-Noor. The mountain of light, the great diamond that came to Lahore from an exiled king, and that the Maharaja wore on his arm. Today's word.
Your line: what is precious. Today, spend ten minutes on the precious thing you chose, not on the things that only shine. Day nine hundred nineteen.

920.title: A court of many faiths
920.hook: a Muslim foreign minister, Hindu and Dogra ministers, and European officers served at his court
920.howItsDone: Sikhs often point to Maharaja Ranjit Singh's court, with its Muslim, Hindu, Dogra, Sikh and European officials, as an example of the Gurus' teaching of one Lord whom Hindus and Muslims each name in their own way.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Koh-i-Noor, the mountain of light, and your line was what is precious. Did you give ten minutes to the thing you chose? Today, the people in the room where the diamond was shown. Day nine hundred twenty.

A foreign visitor at the Lahore court is shown in by a man in a Muslim scholar's dress, who speaks for the kingdom. Across the hall stand Hindu officials who keep the accounts, Dogra brothers from the hills who manage the Maharaja's household, Sikh generals with their turbans and swords, and a few officers in European coats who drill the army. All of them answer to one man. Today: a court of many faiths.
screen: `A MUSLIM SCHOLAR SPEAKS FOR LAHORE.` → `HINDU, DOGRA, SIKH, EUROPEAN.` → `ALL IN ONE HALL.`

segments.voice: Start with the man who spoke for the kingdom. Fakir Azizuddin was a Muslim, a physician and a scholar, and he served the Maharaja as his trusted adviser and envoy. When the British or the Afghans needed to hear from Lahore, he was often the one they heard. Histories remember his tact and his learning. Second, the ministers. The Dogra brothers, Gulab Singh and Dhian Singh among them, rose high at court, and Dhian Singh became chief minister. Hindu officials ran the treasury and the revenue, and Hindu commanders, like the general who took Kashmir, led armies. Third, the soldiers from far away. You've already met the European officers who trained the army. Some of them had served Napoleon, histories say, and they came to Lahore and stayed. And fourth, what holds it together. This was the Sarkar-e-Khalsa, the government in the Khalsa's name, with coins struck in the Gurus' names. Yet the people running it came from many faiths. Sikh tradition points back to the Gurus for the reason. In a hymn of Guru Arjan, the Guru says he is neither Hindu nor Muslim: his body and breath belong to the One whom Hindus call Ram and Muslims call Allah. A court of many faiths fits that old teaching. It wasn't perfect, and the ministers' rivalries will matter later in this story. But the Maharaja chose people for what they could do, and let them keep their own way of praying.
screen: `FAKIR AZIZUDDIN SPEAKS FOR LAHORE.` · `DOGRA AND HINDU MINISTERS.` · `OFFICERS FROM EUROPE.` · `A KHALSA STATE, MANY FAITHS IN IT.` · then, large: `MANY FAITHS, ONE COURT.`

segments.voice: Two minutes with the people you work beside. Sit, and let your breath slow. Bring to mind the people in your daily life who are different from you: different faith, background, age, or way of doing things. Picture them one by one. For each, name one thing they do well, something you'd want on your team. Let the list grow. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.

Fakir Azizuddin, the Muslim physician and envoy who spoke for Lahore, serving a court of many faiths: Dogra and Hindu ministers, Sikh generals and European officers, all serving one Khalsa kingdom. Today's word.
Your line: many faiths, one court. Today, work well with someone who isn't like you. Ask their view first, and use it. Day nine hundred twenty.

921.title: Few executions
921.hook: he is remembered for rarely using the death penalty
921.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Maharaja Ranjit Singh's rare use of the death penalty as part of his legacy, and connect it with the teaching in the Guru Granth Sahib that where there is forgiveness, there is the Lord.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a court of many faiths, with Fakir Azizuddin speaking for Lahore, and your line was many faiths, one court. Whose view did you ask first? Today, what the Maharaja did with the power of life and death. Day nine hundred twenty-one.

A ruler in that age held the power to end a life with a word. A thief, a rebel, a man who tried to kill the king himself. The rope and the sword were close at hand. So it's striking what Ranjit Singh is remembered for. Not the size of his army, this time, or the gold on the Harmandir. He's remembered for how seldom he gave the order. Today: few executions.
screen: `THE POWER TO END A LIFE.` → `THE ROPE AND THE SWORD AT HAND.` → `HE SELDOM GAVE THE ORDER.`

segments.voice: First, the memory. Histories of his reign, including the accounts of foreign visitors, say that the Maharaja rarely used the death penalty, even for serious crimes. Punishment came instead as fines, or loss of office, and sometimes as harsh bodily punishment, which belongs in the honest picture too. But the gallows were not his habit. Second, the stories. Tradition tells of people who attacked or plotted against him and were spared. Whatever the details, the memory is consistent: this was a ruler who would rather keep a man alive. Third, why it matters for a Sikh king. The Gurus taught that the one Lord is in every heart. And among the saloks of Kabir in the Guru Granth Sahib is a short run of pairs: where there is spiritual wisdom, there is righteousness; where there is falsehood, there is sin; where there is greed, there is death; and where there is forgiveness, there is the Lord himself. A ruler who took that seriously would think twice before ending a life. Fourth, mercy is not weakness. Ranjit Singh was no soft ruler. He fought hard, took cities, and kept a tight hold on his kingdom. That's what makes the memory interesting. He had every means to kill and chose, again and again, not to. Mercy means the most in the hands of someone who could do otherwise. That's today's line.
screen: `REMEMBERED FOR RARELY ORDERING DEATH.` · `STORIES OF ENEMIES SPARED.` · `WHERE FORGIVENESS IS, THE LORD IS.` · `MERCY FROM ONE WHO COULD DO OTHERWISE.` · then, large: `MERCY IN POWER.`

segments.voice: Two minutes with mercy. Sit, and let your breath settle. Think of one place where you hold a little power: over a child, a coworker, a sibling, a stranger in a queue, or over yourself. Bring to mind one person in that place who has let you down. Notice what you'd like to do about it. Then, without excusing anything, picture choosing mercy instead, just once. Notice how it feels to hold the power and not use it. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Few executions. The Maharaja who held the power of life and death, and is remembered for how rarely he used it. Today's word.
Your line: mercy in power. Today, when you could be hard on someone and be in the right, choose mercy once. Day nine hundred twenty-one.

922.title: Patna and Nanded
922.hook: he funded buildings at the Tenth Guru's birthplace and resting place
922.howItsDone: Sikhs travel to Takht Sri Patna Sahib and Takht Sri Hazur Sahib at Nanded, the places of Guru Gobind Singh's birth and his final days, and give donations there.

segments.voice: Yesterday, few executions, and your line was mercy in power. Where did you choose mercy, even once? Today, the Maharaja's gifts travel a very long way from Lahore. Day nine hundred twenty-two.

Draw a line on a map of India. Start at Patna, on the Ganges, far to the east. Follow it a long way south and west, down into the Deccan, to Nanded, on the Godavari river. Neither city is in the Punjab. Neither was in Ranjit Singh's kingdom. Yet his money went to both, to build and adorn places that Sikhs travel to. One is where the Tenth Guru was born. The other is where his earthly life ended. Today: Patna and Nanded.
screen: `PATNA, ON THE GANGES.` → `NANDED, ON THE GODAVARI.` → `FAR OUTSIDE HIS KINGDOM.`

segments.voice: First, Patna. Guru Gobind Singh was born there, while his father, Guru Tegh Bahadur, was traveling in the east. The child spent his early years in Patna before the family came to Anandpur. The place of his birth became a gurdwara, and today it's one of the Takhts, the seats of authority Sikhs honor. Second, Nanded. At the end of his life, Guru Gobind Singh traveled south to the Deccan, and it was at Nanded that he gave the Guruship to the Granth and left this world. Sikhs call the gurdwara there Hazur Sahib, and it too is a Takht. Third, the gifts. Histories and gurdwara tradition say Ranjit Singh sent money and craftsmen to both places, to raise and beautify the buildings. He had already covered the Harmandir in gold at Amritsar, inside his own kingdom. These gifts went far beyond his borders, to places he would never rule. That's the point of them. They weren't about holding land. They were about honoring the Guru. And fourth, the line it draws. The Tenth Guru's life ran from the Ganges to the Godavari. A Maharaja in Lahore sent his gifts along that same line, east and south, joining the Punjab to the places where the Guru's life began and ended. Sikhs still travel that line today, and tradition says some of what they see there was paid for from Lahore.
screen: `PATNA, WHERE THE TENTH GURU WAS BORN.` · `NANDED, WHERE HIS EARTHLY LIFE ENDED.` · `GIFTS BEYOND THE KINGDOM'S BORDERS.` · `A LINE FROM THE GANGES TO THE GODAVARI.` · then, large: `GIFTS TO THE GURU'S PLACES.`

Now think of one small gift you could give it: a few coins, an hour of cleaning, flowers, a visit, a word of thanks to whoever keeps it. Just choose it. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Takht, a seat of authority Sikhs honor; Patna and Nanded, the Tenth Guru's birthplace and resting place, are both Takhts, far from Lahore yet both honored with the Maharaja's gifts. Today's word.
Your line: gifts to the guru's places. Today, give the small gift you chose to a sacred place, near or far. Day nine hundred twenty-two.

923.title: Painting at the court
923.hook: Sikh and hill painters made portraits of the court and the Gurus
923.howItsDone: Sikh paintings from the Lahore court era are kept in museums and collections, and some Sikh homes display later pictures of the Gurus; the Sikh code of conduct rejects the worship of images.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Patna and Nanded, both Takhts, and your line was gifts to the guru's places. What small gift did you give? Today, a different kind of gift: pictures. Day nine hundred twenty-three.

Picture a small painting of the kind made for the Lahore court. An old man sits on a cushion in plain clothes, with a white beard, and nothing about him shouts that he's the king. Around him stand courtiers in bright turbans, in reds and golds and greens. No camera ever caught Ranjit Singh. What we have instead is paint, laid on by hand with fine brushes, by artists who worked for his court. Today: painting at the court.
screen: `A SMALL PAINTING.` → `A PLAIN KING AMONG BRIGHT TURBANS.` → `PAINTED FOR THE COURT.`

segments.voice: First, the painters. Some came down from the hill kingdoms north of the Punjab plains, places like Guler and Kangra, with a tradition of small, careful paintings in bright color. As those hill states came under Lahore's power, painters found new patrons at the Sikh court and among its nobles. Sikh artists painted alongside them. Second, what they painted: the court. Portraits of the Maharaja, his sons and his ministers, his generals on horseback, courtiers in a row. Some portraits show the Maharaja himself plainly dressed, among a richly dressed court. Third, what they painted: the Gurus. Painters made portraits of the Gurus, among them Guru Nanak with his companions Bhai Bala and Bhai Mardana, Mardana with his rabab. These images were never photographs. No painter of that time had ever seen the Gurus. The painters were imagining, with devotion, faces they knew only from stories and hymns. Sikhs today hold different views on such pictures. Some hang them in homes with love, some say the Guru is the Word, not a face, and a picture should never become an object of worship. The Sikh code of conduct rejects the worship of images. And fourth, why it matters. These paintings are one way later generations can still see that court: its colors, its clothes, its faces. A kingdom remembered in paint.

924.title: Maharani Jind Kaur
924.hook: his youngest queen, mother of Duleep Singh, would later defy an empire
924.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Maharani Jind Kaur in histories of the end of the Sikh kingdom, and honor her as a mother and queen who would not give in.

segments.voice: Yesterday, painting at the court, with painters from Kangra among them, and your line was the court in paint. What detail did you find in a picture you usually walk past? Today, a face from that court who will matter a great deal. And the week closes. Day nine hundred twenty-four.

A woman's name keeps turning up in the letters of British officials, and not kindly. They write of her as difficult, even dangerous. They try to keep her away from her son. They move her from place to place. Years after the Maharaja is gone, she's still a person they worry about in the Punjab. Who was she? She began as the youngest of the Maharaja's queens. Today: Maharani Jind Kaur.
screen: `A NAME IN OFFICIALS' LETTERS.` → `THEY CALL HER DANGEROUS.` → `THE YOUNGEST QUEEN.`

segments.voice: First, where she came from. Sikh histories say Jind Kaur was the daughter of a man who looked after the royal kennels, not a princess from a great house. She married the Maharaja late in his life, the youngest of his queens. Second, her son. She gave birth to Duleep Singh, the Maharaja's youngest son. When the Maharaja died, the boy was still a baby, far from the throne, with older brothers and powerful ministers between him and it. Few would have guessed he'd ever wear the crown. Third, what's coming. Without spoiling the story ahead: the throne of Lahore would pass through several hands, fast and violently, and in time it reached her son. Then Jind Kaur stood up as regent and spoke for him, in a court full of men and with a foreign empire at the border. She would be separated from him, imprisoned, and still she wouldn't give in. That's what it means to say she defied an empire, and you'll walk through it day by day. Fourth, the week. Look back at the road of these seven days: Peshawar at the edge, the mountain of light, a court of many faiths, a ruler remembered for mercy, gifts sent to the Tenth Guru's places, the court in paint. A kingdom at its height. And standing quietly in it, a young queen whose courage hadn't been tested yet. The Gurus taught that a woman is not less: Guru Nanak asked why anyone would call her lowly, from whom kings are born. Jind Kaur would answer that question in her own way.

segments.voice: Two minutes with a brave mother. Sit, and let your breath settle. Bring to mind a mother who was brave: your own, a grandmother, a friend raising children alone, a mother you've only read about. Picture her face. Think of one hard thing she faced and didn't run from. Hold her in your mind with honor, breath by breath. If she's alive, think of one way you could thank her. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Jind Kaur, the youngest of the Maharaja's queens, mother of Duleep Singh, who would one day stand up to an empire for her son. Today's word.
Your line: a brave queen. Today, honor one brave mother: call her, write to her, or tell someone her story. Day nine hundred twenty-four.
